learn.hook: A village pond and the whole Indian Ocean are both ecosystems. Size changes, but the rules of the game stay the same.
points: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with their surrounding physical environment. Ecosystems vary in size from a small pond to a large forest or sea; many ecologists regard the entire biosphere as a global ecosystem.
Ecosystems are of two basic categories: terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary). Crop fields and an aquarium are man-made ecosystems.
Structure: interaction of biotic and abiotic components gives each ecosystem a characteristic physical structure. Identifying and enumerating plant and animal species gives its species composition.
Stratification is the vertical distribution of different species at different levels. In a forest, trees occupy the top layer, shrubs the second and herbs and grasses the bottom layers.
The components of an ecosystem function as a unit in four ways: productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

example.q: Classify: a mangrove estuary, the Thar desert, a rice field, a home aquarium.
steps: Estuary: natural aquatic ecosystem.
Thar desert: natural terrestrial ecosystem.
Rice field and aquarium: man-made ecosystems.
example.answer: Estuary aquatic; desert terrestrial; rice field and aquarium man-made

learn.reallife: The Sundarbans mangroves of West Bengal and the grasslands of Kutch are very different Indian ecosystems, yet both run on productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

learn.hook: A small village pond is a complete working ecosystem, with producers, consumers, decomposers and the sun powering it all.
points: A pond is a shallow water body showing all the basic components of an ecosystem. Abiotic components: water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances, and rich soil deposit at the bottom. Solar input, temperature cycle, day length and other climate factors regulate the rate of function of the whole pond.
Autotrophs: phytoplankton, some algae, and floating, submerged and marginal plants at the edges.
Consumers: zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms. Decomposers: fungi, bacteria and flagellates, especially abundant at the bottom.

The pond performs all functions of an ecosystem: autotrophs convert inorganic into organic material using solar energy; heterotrophs consume autotrophs; dead organic matter is decomposed and mineralised for reuse by autotrophs, again and again.
Energy moves in one direction towards higher trophic levels and is dissipated and lost as heat to the environment.

example.q: Classify these pond components: phytoplankton, zooplankton, bacteria at the bottom, dissolved minerals, sunlight.
steps: Phytoplankton: autotroph (producer).

example.answer: Phytoplankton producer; zooplankton consumer; bacteria decomposer; minerals and sunlight abiotic

topics.title: Productivity: GPP, NPP and secondary productivity

learn.hook: Oceans cover about 70 per cent of Earth's surface but produce only about a third of its yearly plant biomass.
points: Primary production is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis, expressed as weight (g m⁻²) or energy (kcal m⁻²).
Productivity is the rate of biomass production, expressed as g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹, to compare ecosystems.

Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. A considerable part is used by plants in respiration (R). Net primary productivity: NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers).
Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

Primary productivity depends on plant species, environmental factors, availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity, so it varies among ecosystems. Annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter; the oceans, despite covering about 70 per cent of the surface, produce only about 55 billion tons, and the rest is produced on land.

example.q: A grassland has GPP of 2500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ and respiration losses of 900 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. Find NPP.
steps: NPP = GPP − R.

topics.title: Decomposition: detritus, fragmentation, leaching and catabolism

learn.hook: Earthworms are called the farmer's friend: they shred fallen leaves and loosen soil, starting the recycling of nutrients.
points: Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients: decomposition. Earthworms help break down complex organic matter and loosen the soil, which is why they are called the farmer's friend.
Detritus, the raw material for decomposition, consists of dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead remains of animals, including faecal matter.
Fragmentation: detritivores like earthworms break detritus into smaller particles.
Leaching: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
Catabolism: bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. All these steps operate simultaneously on detritus.

example.q: A fallen neem leaf is first shredded by earthworms, rain carries its soluble salts into the soil, and fungi digest the remains. Name each step.
steps: Shredding by earthworms: fragmentation.
Soluble nutrients washed down: leaching.
Enzymatic breakdown by fungi: catabolism.

topics.title: Humification, mineralisation and factors affecting decomposition

learn.hook: Leaves decompose in a few weeks in a hot, humid Kerala forest, but may lie almost unchanged for years in a cold Himalayan bog.
points: Humification and mineralisation occur during decomposition in soil. Humification leads to accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance called humus, which is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes at an extremely slow rate. Being colloidal, it serves as a reservoir of nutrients.
Mineralisation: humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients.
Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process. Its rate is controlled by the chemical composition of detritus and by climatic factors.
Under a given climate, decomposition is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker if it is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars.

Temperature and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors, acting through their effects on soil microbes. Warm and moist environments favour decomposition; low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, causing build-up of organic material.

example.q: Which will decompose faster under the same climate: a pile of nitrogen-rich, sugary vegetable peels or a pile of woody sawdust rich in lignin? Why?
steps: Lignin-rich detritus decomposes slowly.
Nitrogen- and sugar-rich detritus decomposes quickly.
example.answer: Vegetable peels, because they are rich in nitrogen and soluble sugars, while sawdust is lignin-rich.

learn.reallife: Peat bogs in cold, waterlogged places store huge amounts of carbon because low temperature and lack of oxygen stop decomposition.

learn.hook: Plants capture only a tiny fraction of the sunlight that falls on them, yet that sliver powers every living thing you have ever seen.
points: Except for deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth. Of the incident solar radiation, less than 50 per cent is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).

Plants and photosynthetic bacteria (autotrophs) fix the sun's radiant energy to make food from simple inorganic materials. Plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the PAR, and this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world.

Energy flows in one direction: from the sun to producers and then to consumers. Ecosystems also obey the second law of thermodynamics: they need a constant supply of energy to synthesise required molecules and to counteract the universal tendency towards increasing disorderliness.

Green plants are producers. In terrestrial ecosystems the major producers are herbaceous and woody plants; in aquatic ecosystems they are phytoplankton, algae and higher plants. All animals depend directly or indirectly on plants and are consumers (heterotrophs).

Primary consumers feed on producers (herbivores, e.g. insects, birds and mammals on land and molluscs in water). Secondary consumers (primary carnivores) feed on herbivores; tertiary consumers (secondary carnivores) feed on primary carnivores.

example.q: If 1000 units of solar radiation reach a leaf, at most how much is PAR (taking 50 per cent), and how much might plants capture at 2 per cent and at 10 per cent of this PAR?
steps: PAR is less than 50%: up to 500 units.
2% of 500 = 10 units.
10% of 500 = 50 units.
example.answer: PAR up to 500 units; plants capture about 10–50 units.

learn.reallife: India's solar power parks convert sunlight to electricity at far higher efficiency than plants, but no solar panel can make food, which is why photosynthesis remains irreplaceable.

topics.title: Food chains, food webs and standing crop

learn.hook: In a forest, more energy flows through fallen leaves and the microbes that eat them than through deer and tigers.
points: Grazing food chain (GFC): grass (producer) → goat (primary consumer) → man (secondary consumer). Detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter and is made of decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria. Decomposers are saprotrophs: they secrete digestive enzymes that break dead matter into simple inorganic materials and absorb them.
In aquatic ecosystems, GFC is the major conduit for energy flow. In terrestrial ecosystems, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain.
DFC may connect with GFC: some DFC organisms are prey for GFC animals, and some animals like cockroaches and crows are omnivores. This natural interconnection of food chains makes a food web.

Organisms occupy a specific trophic level based on their source of food: producers first, herbivores second, carnivores third. Energy decreases at successive trophic levels. Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time, the standing crop, measured as biomass (fresh or dry weight; dry weight is more accurate) or number per unit area.

Distinctions for exams: GPP vs NPP (NPP = GPP − R); grazing vs detritus food chain (living producers vs dead organic matter); humification vs mineralisation (humus formation vs nutrient release); and pond components (abiotic, producers, consumers, decomposers).

example.q: Write a grazing food chain from a grassland and name the trophic level of each organism.
steps: Grass (producer): first trophic level.
Grasshopper (herbivore): second trophic level.
Frog (primary carnivore): third trophic level; snake (secondary carnivore): fourth.
example.answer: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake (T1 → T2 → T3 → T4)

learn.reallife: Crows in Indian cities are omnivores: they eat scraps, insects and carrion, linking grazing and detritus food chains into a food web.

topics.title: The 10 per cent law and trophic levels

learn.hook: Of all the energy in the grass a deer eats, only about a tenth ends up in the deer's body. Each step up the chain loses most of the energy.
points: The number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain is restricted because transfer of energy follows the 10 per cent law: only about 10 per cent of the energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower trophic level.
The rest is used in respiration and other life processes or lost as heat. So energy available decreases sharply at each successive level.
In nature it is possible to have levels like producer, herbivore, primary carnivore and secondary carnivore in a grazing food chain, but rarely many more, because too little energy remains.
Calculation method: energy at the next level = energy at the current level × 10/100. Moving up n levels from producers, energy = producer energy × (1/10)ⁿ.

example.q: Producers in a grassland fix 20,000 J of energy. Using the 10 per cent law, how much energy reaches the primary carnivores?
steps: Producers → herbivores: 20,000 × 10/100 = 2000 J.
Herbivores → primary carnivores: 2000 × 10/100 = 200 J.

learn.reallife: This is why a plate of dal-chawal can feed more people per hectare of farmland than meat: eating lower on the food chain loses less energy.

topics.title: Ecological pyramids of number and biomass

learn.hook: In a single banyan tree with thousands of insects, a pyramid of numbers stands on its head.
points: An ecological pyramid has producers (first trophic level) at the base and higher levels on top, with top consumers at the apex. The three types are pyramids of number, biomass and energy.

Any calculation of numbers, biomass or energy must include all organisms at that trophic level. A trophic level represents a functional level, not a species: a sparrow is a primary consumer when it eats seeds and a secondary consumer when it eats insects and worms.

Pyramid of number: generally upright, e.g. in a grassland, where producers are most numerous and top carnivores fewest. In a big tree with many insects feeding on it, the pyramid of numbers is inverted (one tree supporting many insects).

Pyramid of biomass: generally upright in terrestrial ecosystems, showing a sharp decrease in biomass at higher levels. In the sea it is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton (at a given time).

example.q: Why is the pyramid of biomass in the sea generally inverted?
steps: Phytoplankton are tiny and short-lived but reproduce very fast.
At any given time, their standing biomass is less than that of the fishes feeding on them.
So the producer bar is smaller than the consumer bars.
example.answer: The biomass of fishes far exceeds the standing biomass of phytoplankton at a given time.

learn.reallife: In India's coastal waters, fisheries scientists study phytoplankton and fish biomass to understand why small producers can support large fish catches.

topics.title: Pyramid of energy and limitations of pyramids

learn.hook: No matter which ecosystem you choose, the pyramid of energy never stands on its head. Physics forbids it.
points: The pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted, because when energy flows from one trophic level to the next, some energy is always lost as heat at each step. Each bar shows the energy present at that trophic level in a given time or annually per unit area. A primary producer converts only about 1 per cent of the energy in sunlight available to it into NPP.

In most ecosystems all pyramids (number, biomass and energy) are upright: producers exceed herbivores in number and biomass, and herbivores exceed carnivores; energy at a lower level is always more than at a higher level. Exceptions occur for numbers and biomass, but never for energy.

Limitations of ecological pyramids: they do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain, which almost never exists in nature; they do not accommodate a food web; and saprophytes are not given any place even though they play a vital role.
Exam skill: draw pyramids of number, biomass and energy for given ecosystems (grassland, tree, sea), and explain why the energy pyramid is never inverted.
Syllabus note: in the rationalised NCERT book, ecological succession, nutrient cycling (carbon and phosphorus cycles) and ecosystem services are not part of this chapter for the current syllabus.

example.q: A student draws an inverted pyramid of energy for a lake. Explain why this must be wrong.
steps: Energy flows from one trophic level to the next.
At each transfer, some energy is always lost as heat (only about 10% passes on).
So each higher level must have less energy than the one below.
example.answer: An energy pyramid is always upright because energy is lost at every transfer.

learn.reallife: Energy-flow studies in Indian wetlands like Chilika Lake help managers decide how many fish can be harvested sustainably.
